newsitem.title: USA: Leading U.S. Army man charged in sex scandal.
newsitem.headline: Leading U.S. Army man charged in sex scandal.

text.p: The U.S. Army on Wednesday charged its top enlisted soldier with adultery and assault in a case involving four military women in the latest chapter of a sexual harassment scandal that has rocked the service.

The Army said a senior officer would investigate the case against Gene McKinney, the only soldier who carries the venerated military title Sergeant Major of the Army as leading member of the service's highest enlisted rank.

The investigator will decide if the 22-year veteran will face court martial on any of the 18 charges of sexual misconduct and obstruction of justice involving three Army women and a woman sailor over a three-year period.
McKinney denied the charges on Wednesday in an appearance before reporters.

"I want the American people to know, and I certainly want the soldiers of the American Army to know, that I have done no wrong," he said outside his lawyer's office in Alexandria, Va., a Washington suburb.
McKinney, 46, was accompanied by his wife and did not answer questions.
"She supports him fully," McKinney's lawyer, Charles Gittins, told Reuters in an interview. "We will find out why women like these four make false statements like this."
Gittins said McKinney's four accusers were white and he was asked by reporters if he thought that his client, who is black, was the victim of racial prejudice.

"I'm not sure if there's a race issue," the lawyer replied. "I know that in every interview, CID (Army criminal investigators) asked witnesses whether Sgt. Major McKinney was only interested in white women. If there's a race issue it's been injected by the investigators and that's of great concern to me."

McKinney was suspended in February from his Pentagon job as the senior enlisted adviser to service leaders pending resolution of sex harassment allegations lodged against him by former Sgt. Maj. Brenda Hoster.

Hoster, who has retired after 22 years service of her own, alleges she resisted pressure from McKinney to have sex in a hotel room in Hawaii last year while his wife was in another room down the hall.

McKinney is assigned to administrative duties at nearby Fort Myer, Va. A base official said he would remain on the job pending a determination of whether any of the charges might be dismissed and whether he would be tried.
The McKinney case is the latest development in an Army sexual harassment scandal that includes charges of rape of women recruits by drill sergeants at several training bases.

Army Staff Sgt. Delmar Simpson, a key figure in one of the worst U.S. military sex scandals, was sentenced on Tuesday to 25 years in prison for raping six women and other sexual offences at Aberdeen Proving Ground in Maryland.

The Army said the charges against McKinney included four counts each of indecent assault and maltreatment of soldiers, two counts of assault, one count of adultery, two of communicating a threat, two of obstruction of justice and three of soliciting adultery.
The incidents allegedly occurred between October 1994 and March of this year.
Aside from the sexual harassment charges, conviction of adultery by itself may be punished by jail and dismissal from the Army under the Uniform Code of Military Justice.
That code also prohibits sexual relations or even dating between troops of different rank.
